1.note: Nonrestrictive clause needs both commas; B/C drop one, D semicolon leaves a fragment.

2.note: Narrative is past (1858, fled); A is internally consistent present, so passage tense decides.

3.note: Singular possessive of one city; C needs a plural the sentence never has.

4.note: Waste is released on the tide; liberated/emancipated personify, saved is wrong meaning. Plain-word option is key, as in Q37.

5.note: 'whom' is object of 'knew' (colleagues knew him), so No Change is correct; CHECK the key is not C, an author error that would make C keyed and A the right answer.

6.note: Water-pump finding foreshadows waste-free drinking water ending cholera; D's claimed contradiction is false since the 'foul air' belief is attributed to most Londoners.

7.note: Built to remove a smell, yet had an unplanned effect: contrast. Same 'For example' underline appears in Q15 where it is correct.

8.note: 'from which' removes the dangling 'from'; B wrong preposition, C redundant 'it'.

9.note: Comma splice; C still a splice, D makes 'which' clause ungrammatical.

10.note: Pipe doubling is P3; A/C recall P1/P2, B recalls P4. D is also the only choice naming a concrete design act, partly guessable.

12.note: Redundant appositive; B changes the grammar into a dangling modifier.

13.note: Appositive takes a comma; semicolon and period create fragments, D a splice.

14.note: 'complained' plus dictionaries selling out implies hogging; consulting/recommending give no grievance.

15.note: 'Not everyone was charmed' then an instance: For example fits; key is No Change.

16.note: Comma splice; D still a splice.

17.note: PATTERN: key is the sentence already printed as P4's opener (same in Q28), so the passage text gives the key away; D is a weak distractor because P4 is about rules, not her tenure.

19.note: Subject 'rules' is plural; 'along with' phrase does not count; 'still' wants present.

20.note: Example illustrates 'misleads without lying'; A/B/C are visibly false, so it is decidable from the stem.

22.note: Trailing participial phrase set off by comma; B/C fragment; D is borderline (reads as 'slowly molting').

23.note: Noun-clause subject is singular; present matches 'still'.

24.note: Song sentence must follow the males-sing sentence, i.e. before 'The females' = [C].

25.note: Transitive present 'lay'; the sentence is in present tense, so 'laid' is out.

26.note: Swamping predators so most survive is a defense; 'ambush'/'attack' invert the roles.

27.note: Mass emergers survive versus an off-schedule emerger alone: contrast; key is No Change.

28.note: PATTERN as in Q17: the key is the sentence already printed in the passage; A/B/D are off-topic for a paragraph on prime cycles.

29.note: Reflexive refers back to plural 'Thirteen and seventeen'.

30.note: Contrast with subordinator after a comma; D semicolon plus whereas makes a fragment; B is wrong logic.

32.note: Colon introduces the list explaining 'six of us'; the comma blurs the list into a series.

33.note: Coaxing a cat down implies patience; the simile in the stem decides it without the passage.

34.note: Sets up 'For me it was terrifying'; A/B/C are false claims, so D is guessable from the options.

35.note: Colon gives the explanation; B is grammatical (comma + so) and only reverses the cause, so on a stem asking 'most grammatically acceptable' a student can defend it.

36.note: Past perfect for the earlier event before 'realized'.

37.note: 'strong swimmer' is idiomatic; brawny/forceful/mighty are physical-power words. Plain-word option is key (as in Q4).

39.note: Still weak, yet walked into the lake: contrast.

40.note: Personal narrative, not a method; B is unsupported; C/D cite true details that are not step-by-step instructions.
